questions.q: What gap does this lesson close that Lessons 7-9 quietly assumed was already fixed?
options: Whether data is encrypted at rest
Whether query results are masked
Whether Overlook's accounts only have the access they actually need, rather than whatever got granted informally over time
Whether backups exist
questions.explain: Encryption, masking, and auditing all assume some baseline of controlled access — least privilege is what actually establishes that baseline.

questions.q: What is the real difference between `ALTER ROLE db_datareader ADD MEMBER scheduling_app` and granting SELECT on two named tables?
options: They are functionally identical
db_datareader grants read access to every table in the database forever, including future tables; named grants give access to exactly the tables actually needed, and nothing else
Named grants are always slower to execute
db_datareader cannot be used in Azure SQL
questions.explain: The built-in role is broad and open-ended; named object-level grants are narrow and deliberate — the choice that matches least privilege.

questions.q: Why does `reporting_role` get the UNMASK permission while `scheduling_app_role` does not?
options: It's arbitrary and has no real reason

Because reporting_role is the role designed to see real patient values for legitimate reporting work, while scheduling_app_role only needs to read/write appointments and should never see unmasked sensitive columns
UNMASK is required for all database roles
scheduling_app_role cannot technically be granted UNMASK
questions.explain: Only the role that actually needs unmasked data gets UNMASK — by design, not by accident, which is the entire point of least privilege.

questions.q: According to this lesson, when is a built-in role still the genuinely right choice over named object-level grants?
options: Never — named grants are always correct
When an account genuinely needs broad, whole-database access, like a true backup/migration service account or database owner
Only for read-only reporting accounts
Only in non-production environments
questions.explain: Forcing a genuinely broad-access account into a dozen narrow grants would just obscure the fact that it needs broad access anyway.

questions.q: What does this lesson say Overlook's database looks like once Chapter 3 is complete?
options: Fully secured against every possible threat with no further work needed
Encrypted at rest, exposed only to the degree each account actually needs, with a tamper-resistant record of who touched what — ready for Chapter 4's HA/DR to build on
Identical to how it started, with no real change
Ready for a Data Factory pipeline, with no further security needed
questions.explain: TDE, masking, auditing, and least-privilege roles together give Overlook a genuinely secured foundation, which Chapter 4 then protects with HA/DR.
